flashcards.q: Precisely distinguish tokenization, stemming, and lemmatization.
flashcards.a: Tokenization segments text into units, no information loss. Stemming chops affixes via fixed rules, fast, can produce non-words ('universal' -> 'univers'). Lemmatization maps to a dictionary base form using part-of-speech, slower, always produces a real word.

flashcards.q: Give an example a stemmer cannot handle but a lemmatizer can.
flashcards.a: 'better' -> 'good' (adjective comparative to base form) or 'saw' -> 'see' (irregular past tense). Neither has a shared substring for rule-based stemming to exploit; both need dictionary/POS knowledge.

flashcards.q: Why does removing stopwords break phrase search and semantic search?
flashcards.a: Phrase search: removing a stopword can change query meaning entirely ('The Who' minus 'the' becomes just 'Who'). Semantic search: function words like negations ('not') carry structural signal a transformer's attention relies on; removing them can flip a sentence's meaning.

flashcards.q: Derive TF-IDF and explain why a term appearing in every document scores zero.
flashcards.a: TF-IDF(t,d) = TF(t,d) * IDF(t), where IDF(t) = log(N/df(t)). A term in every document has df(t)=N, so IDF = log(1) = 0, contributing nothing — this is algorithmic stopword removal, arrived at by formula instead of a hand-curated list.

flashcards.q: What two corrections does BM25 add over raw TF-IDF, and what do the parameters k1 and b control?
flashcards.a: Term-frequency saturation (k1, typically 1.2-2.0): score approaches k1+1 asymptotically rather than growing linearly with repeated term occurrences. Length normalization (b, typically 0.75): penalizes documents longer than the corpus average, since length alone increases the chance of containing any query term.
BM25(D,Q) = sum over t in Q of: IDF(t) * (f(t,D)*(k1+1)) / (f(t,D) + k1*(1-b+b*|D|/avgdl)), where f(t,D) is term frequency in D, |D| is document length, avgdl is corpus average document length.

flashcards.q: Why did subword tokenization (BPE/WordPiece/SentencePiece) replace whole-word tokenization for neural models?
flashcards.a: Whole-word tokenization collapses any out-of-vocabulary word into an unrecoverable <UNK> token, destroying information. Character-level has no OOV problem but produces very long sequences, wasting capacity relearning word structure. Subword tokenization keeps common words as single tokens, decomposes rare words into meaningful pieces, and has no true OOV case.

flashcards.q: What is mojibake and where does it silently break a retrieval pipeline?
flashcards.a: Mojibake is garbled text from decoding with the wrong character encoding (e.g. 'Ã©' instead of 'é'). It shows up as documents that tokenize/embed into meaningless garbage — a garbage lexical index entry, or an embedding vector for noise instead of content — with no thrown error.

flashcards.q: Why does NFC vs NFD Unicode normalization cause silent retrieval failures, and where should normalization happen?
flashcards.a: The same visual character (e.g. 'é') can have multiple valid byte representations (precomposed NFC vs base+combining-mark NFD) — visually identical but byte-different, so exact-match or hashing treats them as different strings. Normalize to NFC (or NFKC) at the ingestion boundary, applied consistently to both the query and document paths, before tokenization or hashing.

flashcards.q: Your team adds lowercase/stem/strip-punctuation preprocessing ahead of a dense embedding model and retrieval quality drops. Why?
flashcards.a: The embedding model was trained on natural, unmodified text. Feeding it stemmed non-words, lowercased text, or punctuation-stripped text produces token sequences and structure patterns it never saw in training, degrading embedding quality silently — the model still returns a vector, just a worse one.

flashcards.q: Why is a classical stem-then-search pipeline a specific risk for a 22-locale product?
flashcards.a: Stemmers/lemmatizers are hand-built per-language resources; high-quality coverage exists for only a few dozen languages, with none at all for many others. A pipeline whose correctness depends on stemming has silently uneven quality per locale, usually undiscovered until a locale-specific bug report.

flashcards.q: Give an example of a term that should NOT be stemmed, and why.
flashcards.a: An exact identifier like a SKU code or 'iOS17' — stemming rules aren't aware of identifier semantics and can mangle the string so it no longer matches the literal text, destroying the exact match that identifier-style lexical search depends on.

flashcards.q: What's the correct amount of preprocessing for a pipeline feeding a dense embedding model?
flashcards.a: Close to none: Unicode-normalize (NFC), strip genuine non-content artifacts (control characters, encoding errors), and otherwise feed text as close to its natural form as possible — no stemming, no stopword removal, no aggressive case folding.
